title: Replication strategies in depth
problem: The primary dies with acknowledged commits still unsent, a forgotten replication slot fills the disk, or two regions update the same row and one write quietly disappears.
summary: Replication ships statements, physical WAL or logical row changes, each with different limits. Slots keep lagging replicas fed, failover trades a data-loss window against commit latency, multi-leader setups need LWW, merges or CRDTs, and CDC turns the log into events.
catTip: I follow the human from room to room by the sound of footsteps: that is physical replication, exact but same-house only. A note saying the bowl moved to the kitchen works in any house. That is logical.

recall.q: A primary with asynchronous standbys crashes. What exactly is lost, and which setting would have prevented it, at what cost?
recall.a: Every transaction the primary acknowledged after the promoted standby's last received WAL position: the data-loss window equals the replication lag. A non-empty synchronous_standby_names makes commits wait for standby confirmation, closing the window at the price of latency and of commits hanging if the standbys are down.

guide.breaks: Ship statements and non-deterministic functions make replicas diverge; recycle WAL a lagging replica still needs and it must be rebuilt; promote a standby without fencing the old primary and two servers accept conflicting writes.
guide.tradeoffs: Physical replication is exact but version-locked, logical replication is flexible but skips DDL and bloats on bulk changes, slots can fill disks, and synchronous commits buy zero loss with latency and availability risk.
guide.explainSimply: Keeping a copy of a database means sending every change somewhere else, and you can send the instruction, the exact bytes, or a plain description of what changed, like mailing a recipe, a frozen kitchen, or a shopping list. If the original fails, a copy takes over, and whatever had not arrived yet is lost. If two copies both accept changes, you need a rule for who wins.
guide.hint: Think about what was acknowledged but not yet sent, and about what crosses the wire in each style.

meow: Statement, WAL bytes, or row changes: three ways to copy. Fence the old primary before the new one purrs, or two cats claim the same bowl.

quiz.prompt: Why is statement-based replication unsafe for UPDATE accounts SET token = UUID() WHERE id = 7?
options: UPDATE statements cannot be written to a binary log
UUID() is non-deterministic, so each replica computes a different value; row-based replication ships the resulting row instead
The WHERE clause is not replicated
quiz.explanation: Statement replay re-evaluates the function on each server, while row-based logging records the resulting row image so every copy matches. The WHERE clause is sent fine; it is the computed value that differs.

quiz.prompt: A team ran a Debezium connector for a week-long test, then stopped it without dropping its PostgreSQL replication slot. What happens over the following weeks?
options: Nothing; unused slots are removed automatically
The primary retains all WAL the slot has not consumed, and with the default unlimited max_slot_wal_keep_size the disk eventually fills
Logical replication to other subscribers speeds up
The primary refuses new connections immediately
quiz.explanation: A slot is a promise to keep WAL until its consumer reads it, connected or not, and only max_slot_wal_keep_size caps that, defaulting to unlimited. Slots are never dropped automatically for being idle.

cards.q: Compare physical and logical replication in PostgreSQL on three axes: what is shipped, version compatibility, and what the replica can do.
cards.a: Physical ships WAL records addressed by block and produces a byte-identical read-only standby that must run the same major version. Logical ships row changes keyed by replication identity to a subscriber that can run another major version, hold a subset of tables, keep its own indexes and accept writes, but DDL is not replicated.

cards.q: Two regions each accept writes to the same shopping cart while the link between them is down. Give three ways to reconcile when it returns and one drawback of each.
cards.a: Last writer wins by timestamp (simple, but discards a write and trusts clocks); keep both versions and let the application merge (correct but pushes complexity to developers, and deleted items can reappear); use a CRDT such as a set type (merges automatically, but only for data that fits a CRDT shape).

glossary.note: Reading a database's log and publishing each row change as an event for other systems.
A data structure whose concurrent updates on different replicas merge deterministically without coordination.
